items.title: A lot of business owners, founders and CEOs now need to have the difficult conversation with themsel...
items.content:
A lot of business owners, founders and CEOs now need to have the difficult conversation with themselves that their business simply doesn't have a reason to exist anymore in this new era

I think the types of businesses (and people) that succeed in a post-AGI era might just be completely different

You understand better now the extremely aggressive pivots to AI many companies a few years ago did, completely resetting their company or rebuilding it from scratch after they realized this

I remember Replit for example was just an online IDE that you could use with other people (targeted to coders), it got big with coding teachers, then in 2024 @amasad hard pivoted it to be an AI app and site generator target to the opposite audience: non-coders, which caused lots of backlash, but that worked, now it's projected to hit $1B ARR by end of this year!

Anyway, we're in a completely new era with completely different dynamics for what businesses will survive and which will perish, what worked last year might not work this year anymore, and what works this year might not work next year anymore, because we're dealing with AI models that get exponentially better every year

@josiah_arcanist @_catwu I don't think Ant is the only lab that's going to build safe AI, and I don't think that'd be the ideal outcome for anyone.

I do really believe in 'the race to the top', which Ant has done an incredible job of creating (or "hyperstitioning"), for example by showing that alignment is core to making models work, for both safety and commercial reasons.

But we need to race to the top across many dimensions, and a healthy race requires many good faith participants in it.

items.content: I’ve spent a better part of the past 2-3 months collaborating with an old friend of mine who is a math professor. We’ve been working on some research using AI, primarily Astra. Solving problems in his speciality that have been open for decades or even longer. We are having a blast. He and his other collaborators are well established in their jobs, not seeking to climb any more academic career ladders. I am completely outside the academic professional/status games, and am just grateful to be learning about something new and pushing the envelope of knowledge for its own sake. Some of that work we’ve submitted to the “traditional” publishing venues, but most we’ll release publicly in the upcoming weeks, probably on GitHub.

items.title:
MATS rejects 98-99% of applicants. But you don't even need a degree to get in.

CEO @ryan_kidd44 bre...
items.content:
MATS rejects 98-99% of applicants. But you don't even need a degree to get in.

CEO @ryan_kidd44 breaks down what actually separates successful applicants, from coding with AI agents to exceptional research ability:

"The median person is about 26 or 27 who gets into our fellowship program. About 15% are undergrads. About 15% have PhDs already. Basically, we just want the best, and we don't care about your credentials."

"Just give it a shot, and if it doesn't work, I highly recommend SPAR and BlueDot for amazing courses and 80,000 Hours for just getting a job and getting in the door."

"You might as well ask what does it take to get into MIT. We have about a 1% or 2% selection rate for our main program. For the empirical tracks, you're gonna want to be really damn good at coding fast and effectively. And that means using AI systems as much as possible, chaining them together, having many agents running in parallel."

"We do have interviews for many of our tracks, and what we're trying to look for is mission alignment, social competence, because these are gonna be more and more important in the job market as AI agents automate from the bottom up."

"Ideally, have a couple first author papers if you can at NeurIPS, ICLR or ICML. If that's not you, I've headhunted people before who were extraordinarily cracked. You can just get out there and do cool stuff without a degree."
@MATSprogram

items.title: If I have Bluetooth enabled on my MacBook Pro, Chrome will request a list of paired Bluetooth device...
items.content:
If I have Bluetooth enabled on my MacBook Pro, Chrome will request a list of paired Bluetooth devices 27 times per second, freezing my computer every 3 seconds

About 15,000+ requests per minute

This is Chrome 158.0.8127.37

@ChromiumDev 

From my clanker: "Chrome is doing the same thing I found on Nov 11, and it's happening right now. It isn't caused by your superlevels extension, which has no Bluetooth code.

What I measured just now (30 seconds of the Bluetooth service's log):
- Chrome asked macOS for your list of paired devices about 27 times a second.
- It asked for the state of individual devices about 190 times a second, roughly 7 devices on every pass.
- That's about 15,000+ requests from Chrome per minute. Every other app combined sent about 60.
- bluetoothd, the macOS Bluetooth service, is at 59% CPU because of it.

Why Chrome does this: Chrome keeps track of paired Bluetooth devices for passkey sign-in with your phone and for websites that connect to Bluetooth devices. Normally it checks every so often. Here it's stuck in a loop and checks dozens of times a second. No extension or Chrome flag is causing it, so it looks like a Chrome bug. On Nov 11 it started right after a Bluetooth device disconnected, and it has probably been stuck again since a disconnect at some point. Chrome has been running for 4.5 days."

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Dario Amodei says it's "absurd" to suggest he wants humans to surrender free wi...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Dario Amodei says it's "absurd" to suggest he wants humans to surrender free will to AI

• Dario draws a line between AI governing society, which he calls "a terrible idea," and AI automating tasks like driving cars, designing cancer drugs or writing software end to end.

• On automation, he sets out four limits: RSI, job disruption, trusting AI with alignment research, and things people would rather do themselves.

• He cites Anthropic's refusal to let its models be used for fully autonomous weapons, a stand that got the company put on a government blacklist.

• Anthropic already said in its Nov 2 IPO filing that it doesn't expect to safely use Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously.

• People familiar with company discussions still told Axios that the belief AI will take over human decision-making is common inside Anthropic.

• Meta's @alexandr_wang wrote that society shouldn't accept a "handover" to AI, and @sama said he wants people to keep "agency over the future."

@theojaffee: "Dario says that he is opposed to AI labs usurping power. I think he's opposed to other AI labs usurping power. If the people at Anthropic were handed the One Ring, do you think they would throw it into the fire? Like, I'm just not convinced of that."

• Axios re...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Should superintelligent AI make life-or-death decisions for humans?

• Axios reported that a common view inside Anthropic holds that humanity should hand some decision-making power to superintelligent AI, and that rival AI leaders are increasingly pushing back.

• Amodei has said AI should take over life-critical decisions, oversee research and potentially distribute economic resources.

• He has also said fully autonomous weapons may one day be needed to defend democracy if adversaries build them.

• A product vision slide from several years ago, revealed in litigation, described Anthropic's vision for a better world as a "utopia ruled by God in a box."

• @deanwball calls the quiet acceptance of ceding control to AI the "silent consensus."

• Anthropic told Axios that Amodei has advocated for human control of AI and that it trains Claude not to undermine human oversight.

@theojaffee: "Would you rather have a human doctor operate on you because they're a human or a far superior robot doctor? I think everyone in that situation would choose the robot doctor. There are no atheists in a foxhole, right? There are no human supremacists in the trauma ward."

items.title:
Imagine a robot walking in a museum and mapping everything it sees.

The robot uses every camera fra...
items.content:
Imagine a robot walking in a museum and mapping everything it sees.

The robot uses every camera frame to estimate where it is and build a 3D representation.

But generating a good map is hard: every small error can accumulate as the robot moves, causing the map to gradually drift out of alignment.

@robbyant_brain addresses this with LingBot-Map 2.0:

It's a model that takes video and estimates the camera's path and the scene's 3D geometry frame by frame.

This version has a new feature: Refine, and the way it works is pretty cool:

• Refine updates the geometric context the model uses to estimate the camera trajectory.

• It saves those updates to the model so it can improve existing reconstructions and use the updated geometry to process future frames.

• You can trigger Refine at any point during a run to reduce accumulated drift.

And all of this happens inside the model, without any external optimization backend.

Look at the attached demo:

• The orange path is the estimated camera trajectory before Refine.
• The cyan path shows the corrected trajectory after Refine.

This is one of the key capabilities supporting the embodied-native, general-purpose robot brain @robbyant_brain is building. Without reliable spatial memory, autonomous work over large areas and long hours isn't possible.

Here is more information about the model:

• Project page: https://t.co/6eOgPpXAmV

• Technical report: https://t.co/CLKWm7l384

• GitHub: https://t.co/boWEZ4hH1t

• Hugging Face: https://t.co/7r3UTMRwWv

The Streaming version is open source; Refine is not included.

items.title: Nuro has begun fully driverless testing on public roads in the Bay Area, bringing its robotaxi partn...
items.content:
Nuro has begun fully driverless testing on public roads in the Bay Area, bringing its robotaxi partnership with Lucid and Uber one step closer to a Q1 2027 commercial launch.

Nuro COO Andrew Chapin explains why achieving superhuman safety remains the biggest bottleneck to scaling autonomous vehicles:

"The bar is not human-level safety, it is superhuman safety."

"If you are going to build a service with hundreds or thousands and beyond vehicles on the road in a fully driverless capacity, you have to be incredibly safe so as to not rack up a large number of incidents."

"Getting to the point where you can really scale requires, A, superhuman performance, B, a whole lot of capital, C, a vehicle program that can actually scale because you still have to produce physical cars."

items.title: MATS Research CEO @ryan_kidd44 says NIST's CAISSI has a budget of just ~$10 million and argues it sh...
items.content:
MATS Research CEO @ryan_kidd44 says NIST's CAISSI has a budget of just ~$10 million and argues it should receive hundreds of millions.

He warns that AI risks could far exceed today's cybersecurity threats, and says Washington could mobilize billions to prepare:

"I've been very bad at predicting the Trump administration before, so there's maybe some high variance here. But I'm quite happy to see Trump and Xi Jinping talking about guardrails and joint slowing plans."

"We have this fantastically resourced UK AI Security Institute. In the US, we have CAISSI under NIST, and as I understand, their budget is nothing. It's like maybe 10 million or something. That's the first thing to fix. They should give several hundred million dollars, like the UK has done."

"DARPA has this AI Forge program. It's targeting control, robustness, and interpretability. I love those words. If they wanted to, they could easily move billions in a year."

"My hope is that the spending from governments at least keeps pace with the size of interest and growth in the field. That would mean a 2X-ing per year. That would be my median prediction if they were serious about it."
@MATSprogram

items.title: Frontier AI companies are spending an estimated $2.5 billion on safety and security. But MATS Resear...
items.content:
Frontier AI companies are spending an estimated $2.5 billion on safety and security. But MATS Research CEO @ryan_kidd44 thinks they're still missing something.

He questions why Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and OpenAI aren't investing more in dedicated mathematical AI safety research teams:

"Having access to the biggest and best toys at the frontier AI companies is a really damn good way, a massive accelerant of research in general. Hopefully, they're pouring a bunch of those resources into AI safety and security."

"I know of a few people who are doing mathematical AI safety at the frontier at Google DeepMind, Marcus Hutter, Tom Everitt. These guys are kings. But as far as I'm aware, they've outsourced most of their supporting teams to external infrastructure."

"Why doesn't GDM give them the money, the headcount, to just build stacked mathematics teams to solve these maths problems? And where's the Anthropic, OpenAI teams for this?"

"Even though 2.5 billion sounds like a lot, clearly we could do more. The frontier AI companies could spend a ton more, and they probably should."
@MATSprogram

"I know of a few people who are doing mathematical AI safety at the frontier at Google DeepMind, Marcus Hutter, Tom Everitt. These guys are kings. But as far as I'm aware, they've outsourced most of their supporting teams to external infrastructure."

"Why doesn't GDM give them the money, the headcount, to just build stacked mathematics teams to solve these maths problems? And where's the Anthropic, OpenAI teams for this?"

"Even though 2.5 billion sounds like a lot, clearly we could do more. The frontier AI companies could spend a ton more, and they probably should."

@MATSprogram

items.content: @ArczTM Reining in RSI isn't about regulating open models, it's entirely about regulating frontier labs, those are the places where recursive self-improvement will happen. ...
items.content:
Let me try to explain why I'm in favor of blocking AI replies, and I love what @levelsio is doing. 

I'll answer every single one of your points:

> "The cure is worse than the disease."

I gave up on my comment section a few months ago because AI replies ran it over. Since I started blocking these spammers aggressively, I can now read real humans again.

This cure is way better *to me* than the disease.  You don't have to participate or like it, but this has improved my experience on this platform by 200%.

> A public blocklist fed by anyone tagging a bot turns every thread into a tribunal

The list doesn't automatically add the accounts you report. First, every account gets verified, and it's only marked as spam after many AI-looking replies.

If an account is reported and that person doesn't post AI-generated slop, the account will never be added to the block list.

> accusations with no due process

This is not the case. Even if you get added to the blocklist, you can request removal, and you will, as long as you stop posting AI-generated slop.

> and real people listed as "AI spammers" for life

Again, this isn't true for the reasons I explained above.

> AI replies are annoying

No, they aren't just annoying; they are literally the death of this platform.

> A crowd hunting them is dangerous.

It is dangerous! To those ruining this for everyone else.

To get monetized on X you need:
- 500+ active verified followers

They think spamming reply sections will get them more followers and then main timeline impressions maybe because X only pays for timeline impressions not replies anymore

But it's dumb because almost nobody passes that even

Then their scheme is either getting paid content partnerships posts from companies, or selling their accounts

That only works economically if they make hundreds of accounts and spam all of them

But it's fake engagement and spam and a short cut

Silicon Valley started with a series of tunnels for Leland Stanford to complete the transcontinental railroad, which resulted in a monopoly.

He had the only way to move goods across America.

At CES next month these tunnels will give a quarter million rides.

But who goes to Vegas?

People from all over the world.

The tunnels are very important to selling autonomous vehicles to the world.

It is where many people will have their first ride in one.

And only autonomous vehicles will be allowed in them.

items.content:
@elonmusk Silicon Valley started with a series of tunnels for Leland Stanford to complete the transcontinental railroad, which resulted in a monopoly.

He had the only way to move goods across America.

At CES next month these tunnels will give a quarter million rides.

But who goes to Vegas?

People from all over the world.

The tunnels are very important to selling autonomous vehicles to the world.

It is where many people will have their first ride in one.

And only autonomous vehicles will be allowed in them.

items.title: Why Data Science Projects Fail — The Harsh Realities of Implementing AI and Analytics, without the H...
items.content:
Why Data Science Projects Fail — The Harsh Realities of Implementing AI and Analytics, without the Hype (Chapman & Hall/CRC Data Science Series): https://t.co/DA6rLZBlz6

AMAZON SUMMARY:

The field of artificial intelligence, data science, and analytics is crippling itself. Exaggerated promises of unrealistic technologies, simplifications of complex projects, and marketing hype are leading to an erosion of trust in one of our most critical approaches to making decisions: data driven.

This book aims to fix this by countering the AI hype with a dose of realism. Written by two experts in the field, the authors firmly believe in the power of mathematics, computing, and analytics, but if false expectations are set and practitioners and leaders don’t fully understand everything that really goes into data science projects, then a stunning 80% (or more) of analytics projects will continue to fail, costing enterprises and society hundreds of billions of dollars, and leading to non-experts abandoning one of the most important data-driven decision-making capabilities altogether.

For the first time, business leaders, practitioners, students, and interested laypeople will learn what really makes a data science project successful. By illustrating with many personal stories, the authors reveal the harsh realities of implementing AI and analytics.

items.content_html:
Why Data Science Projects Fail — The Harsh Realities of Implementing AI and Analytics, without the Hype (Chapman & Hall/CRC Data Science Series): https://t.co/DA6rLZBlz6

AMAZON SUMMARY:

The field of artificial intelligence, data science, and analytics is crippling itself. Exaggerated promises of unrealistic technologies, simplifications of complex projects, and marketing hype are leading to an erosion of trust in one of our most critical approaches to making decisions: data driven.

This book aims to fix this by countering the AI hype with a dose of realism. Written by two experts in the field, the authors firmly believe in the power of mathematics, computing, and analytics, but if false expectations are set and practitioners and leaders don’t fully understand everything that really goes into data science projects, then a stunning 80% (or more) of analytics projects will continue to fail, costing enterprises and society hundreds of billions of dollars, and leading to non-experts abandoning one of the most important data-driven decision-making capabilities altogether.

For the first time, business leaders, practitioners, students, and interested laypeople will learn what really makes a data science project successful. By illustrating with many personal stories, the authors reveal the harsh realities of implementing AI and analytics.

"Vector: A Surprising Story of Space, Time, and Mathematical Transformation"

Find it here: https://...
items.content:
"Vector: A Surprising Story of Space, Time, and Mathematical Transformation"

Find it here: https://t.co/6vomnSF3Jq

Amazon description:

A celebration of the seemingly simple idea that allowed us to imagine the world in new dimensions—sparking both controversy and discovery. 

Vector and tensor calculus offers an elegant language for expressing the way things behave in space and time, and Robyn Arianrhod shows how this enabled physicists and mathematicians to think in a brand-new way. These include James Clerk Maxwell when he ushered in the wireless electromagnetic age; Einstein when he predicted the curving of space-time and the existence of gravitational waves; Paul Dirac, when he created quantum field theory; and Emmy Noether, when she connected mathematical symmetry and the conservation of energy. 

It turned out that it’s not just physical quantities and dimensions that vectors and tensors can represent, but other dimensions and other kinds of information, too. This is why physicists and mathematicians can speak of four-dimensional space-time and other higher-dimensional “spaces,” and why you’re likely relying on vectors or tensors whenever you use digital applications such as search engines, GPS, or your mobile phone.

items.content:
Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch): https://t.co/IzY3D4m8nG by @rasbt via @ManningBooks 
🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟
Amazon summary:

The book is especially useful because it implements the core methods from scratch rather than treating them as black-box library calls. Readers see how self-consistency, self-refinement, Best-of-N, and training-based methods actually work, including their cost and latency trade-offs. 

The book also discusses common failure modes, including cases where refinement can make answers worse. Difficult concepts such as softmax, temperature, and top-p sampling are clarified with code-linked explanations and diagrams, while visual workflows make pipelines and scoring methods easier to follow.

Reading the book feels like following a guided technical build rather than a loose survey of AI topics. Each concept is introduced because the project now needs it. Diagrams, roadmaps, code listings, exercises, and repeated workflow summaries help readers stay oriented through advanced material.

“One of the biggest shifts happening in our industry is that enterprise data management is expanding into enterprise knowledge management. AI is accelerating that transition because it depends on more than well-managed data. It depends upon context, shared meaning, trusted relationships, and the ability to organize the vast stores of unstructured knowledge that exist across every large enterprise. As AI becomes the primary interface to enterprise information, knowledge management will become the foundation that unlocks trustworthy AI at scale.”

Instead of treating ontology development or knowledge graph construction as a black box, this book provides a clear sequence: controlled vocabularies, metadata schemas, taxonomies, thesauri, ontologies, and knowledge graphs.”

@JasonRute i wasn’t defending her main point and could have been clearer.

also: my understanding is that mathematicians generally care about elegance; sure that’s a value judgement but people seem very eager to suspend that value in the context and i think (and Terence Tao thinks) we should still have some respect for that value.

i am a scientist rather than mathematician but certainly don’t wish my fields to be overcome with uninterpretable and wildly messy but correct observations.

Gaussian, also known as the Mathematics Prince, was a German mathematician from 1847 who made significant contributions to many fields in mathematics and science. Gaussian displayed extraordinary intellectual abilities from a young age. His work laid the foundation for numerous areas of mathematics and science, and his influence is still felt today.

Gauss's prodigious talent was evident early on. By the age of three years, he had reportedly corrected an error in his father's payroll calculations. His formal education began at the age of seven, and he quickly surpassed his peers. Recognizing his potential, the Duke of Brunswick sponsored his education, allowing Gauss to attend the Collegium Carolinum and later the University of Göttingen.

During his time at university, Gauss made several groundbreaking discoveries, including the construction of a regular 17-sided polygon using only a compass and straightedge, a feat that had eluded mathematicians for centuries.

Contributions to Mathematics

Gaussian’s contributions to mathematics are vast and varied, spanning several key areas:

Number Theory:

Gauss's work in number theory is perhaps his most celebrated. His book Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, published in 1801, is a seminal work that systematized number theory and introduced several important concepts, including modular arithmetic and the notion of congruence. He also proved the fundamental theorem of algebra, which states that every non-constant polynomial equation has at least one complex root.

Statistics and Probability:

Gauss made significant contributions to statistics, particularly in the development of the method of least squares, which is used to minimize the differences between observed and predicted values. This method is fundamental in statistical regression analysis. The Gaussian distribution, or normal distribution, is named after him and is a cornerstone of probability theory and statistics.

Geometry and Differential Geometry:

Gauss's work in geometry includes the development of the Gaussian curvature, a concept that measures the intrinsic curvature of a surface. His Theorema Egregium ("Remarkable Theorem") demonstrated that curvature is an intrinsic property of a surface, independent of its embedding in three-dimensional space. This work laid the groundwork for the later development of differential geometry.

Astronomy and Physics:

Gauss applied his mathematical genius to astronomy, predicting the position of the dwarf planet Ceres using his method of least squares. His work in physics includes contributions to the study of magnetism, where he developed the Gauss's law for magnetism, Maxwell's equations that form the foundation of classical electromagnetism.

Complex Analysis:

Gauss made significant contributions to complex analysis, particularly in the theory of complex numbers. He was rigorously defined complex numbers and their operations, and he contributed to the understanding of functions of a complex variable.

Legacy and Impact

Gauss's influence extends beyond his specific contributions to mathematics and science. His rigorous approach to problem-solving and his ability to synthesize disparate areas of mathematics have inspired generations of mathematicians. Many mathematical concepts, theorems, and terms bear his name, including Gaussian elimination, Gaussian integers, and the Gauss-Bonnet theorem.

In addition to his mathematical prowess, Gauss was known for his humility and dedication to his work. He continued to contribute to mathematics and science until his death on February 23, 1855. His legacy is preserved not only in the numerous concepts and theorems named after him but also in the continued relevance of his work in modern mathematics and science.

In conclusion, Gauss was a towering figure in the history of mathematics. His mathematics, is known as, ‘Gaussian.’ His contributions have had a profound and lasting impact on a wide range of fields, from number theory and statistics to geometry and physics. Gauss's work exemplifies the power of mathematical thought and its ability to illuminate the natural world, making him a central figure in the development of modern science.

References

Tent, M. B. W. (2006). The prince of mathematics: Carl Friedrich Gauss. A K Peters. https://t.co/Epkj4hw2eY

Gauss, C. F. (1801). Disquisitiones arithmeticae. https://t.co/HqeTl9bRQR

I'm now in Dubai where if you ask to pay, they're at ...
items.content:
@Pekkagaiser @peturgeorgievv Just to compare:

I'm now in Dubai where if you ask to pay, they're at your table with a payment terminal within 30 seconds, you tap your card, 1 second later it's paid, you're out

Then you order an Uber, it's there in 1 minute, you enter the Uber where you set (silent, no music, cool AC) and it is literally silent, no music and cool AC

In Portugal just paying in a cafe/restaurant takes 15-30 minutes, you get rude service, then you try order a Uber and it takes ages and they cancel on you all the time, if you do get one the car smells, is dirty, the driver will complain about his life and use you as therapy or play loud music and he'll not use AC instead opening the windows and you'll be sweating your ass off

It's all just so primitive man, it doesn't have to be like this at all
